approachQuestion.prompt:
Find a retained badge

A read-only random-access array `badges` was strictly increasing, then rotated by moving a prefix to the end (possibly an empty prefix). All integers are distinct. Given `target`, return its current index, or -1 if absent.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; values and target are signed 32-bit integers. Prefer the method with the asymptotically smallest worst-case number of array probes, then the least working memory.

Examples: badges=[40,55,8,17,29], target=17 -> 3; target=41 -> -1; badges=[8], target=8 -> 0.
constraints: All values are distinct; rotation preserves each original value exactly once.
The original array and rotation offset are not provided.

options.text: Iterate over an inclusive index interval. Check the midpoint for equality. Determine which half is sorted by comparing the left endpoint with the midpoint; retain that half only if target lies within its value bounds, otherwise retain the other half.
options.feedback: Distinct values ensure at least one half is ordered. Its endpoints decide whether it can contain target, so discarding the other half preserves any match.

options.text: First locate the minimum by iterative binary search comparing midpoint with the right endpoint. Then binary-search the appropriate sorted side for target, without copying.
options.feedback: The minimum identifies the rotation boundary. Both resulting ranges are sorted, and two successive interval searches have the same asymptotic probe and memory bounds as the direct search.

options.text: Use the ordered-half rule, but recursively pass a copied retained slice and carry its original index offset.
options.feedback: The rule and offset return the correct current index, but copying a retained half adds avoidable work and storage. Index bounds remove that cost.

options.text: Apply ordinary increasing-array binary search to the whole array, moving right whenever midpoint is below target.
options.feedback: For [40,55,8,17,29] and target 55, midpoint 8 sends the search right and discards the answer at index 1.

feedback.reason: Check equality first. If left through midpoint is sorted, keep its interior only when target lies from the left value up to but excluding the midpoint value. Otherwise search right. When the right half is sorted, use its corresponding bounds. Update indices iteratively; an empty interval means absent.

A rotated array still has a sorted half at each step under the distinct-value contract. Check whether target lies inside that half before choosing it; blindly applying ordinary sorted-array bounds can discard the target.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only ordered-half: the iterative direct search using inclusive bounds, with no slices or recursion. Let n be badges.length. Array access and fixed-width comparisons take constant time; bounds use overflow-safe arithmetic. Choose the tightest pair.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: Constant-work probes discard half the remaining distinct rotated interval.
details: Each iteration uses a fixed number of endpoint probes to identify a sorted half and discard half the interval. Therefore there are O(log(n+1)) iterations, each with constant work and the same scalar indices.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Each iteration discards about half the candidate indices; only scalar bounds are stored.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Sorted-half elimination halves the distinct rotated interval, rather than scanning every value.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(log(n + 1)) auxiliary space”: Only iterative low/high/mid indices are retained; no recursive chain grows with search depth.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A target can require repeated midpoint decisions across logarithmically many intervals, not one probe.
